lesson.grammar_point: mandative subjunctive in suggestions and recommendations

listenings.text: Good evening, and welcome to the debate evening. A few rules before we start, and they are short. Each speaker has four minutes, not five, and I will stop you at four. After both speakers, the floor is open, and the only condition I insist on is that every objection be addressed to the argument and not to the person who made it. If you want to come in, raise a hand and wait. Do not talk over anybody, because the recording picks up nothing when two people speak at once and half the room hears nothing either. The motion tonight is that this country spends too little on public transport. Our first speaker proposes it, our second opposes it, and I would ask that the vote be taken at the end rather than now.

There is one move that changes how you are heard in English, and it costs you nothing. Before you disagree, concede something. One thing, and it has to be true. That is a fair point about the cost. You are right that nobody has explained the timing. Then you push back on the rest. What makes this work is not politeness, and I would say that most learners get this wrong. It works because it proves you were listening, and a room gives its attention to somebody who has just demonstrated that. The mistake to avoid is conceding something nobody claimed, which is a straw man and everybody can see it. And the second mistake is conceding everything, because then you have simply agreed and the conversation stops. One true, limited point. Then the word but, and then your argument.

extra_audio.text: Judith tells Braulio that he was right in the debate and that he lost the room anyway. He answers that he had the figures and that nobody argued with them. Judith explains that he corrected the speaker in the first sentence, before conceding anything at all. Braulio asks her what he was supposed to concede when the man was wrong. She tells him to concede one small true thing first, because that is what buys him the right to be listened to.

reading.rtitle: Why They Agree With You Before They Disagree
paras: The most confusing sentence in an argument in English is the one that sounds like surrender. That is a fair point. I take your point. You may well be right. A Portuguese speaker hears agreement and relaxes, and forty seconds later discovers that nothing was conceded at all.

What is happening is a move, and it appears in every debating handbook. You concede the smallest true thing the other side has said, you do it out loud, and only then do you push back on the rest. The cost is nothing, because the point you gave away was never the point. The gain is large, because you have demonstrated that you were listening, and that is what buys you the right to be listened to.

The move only works if what you concede is real. Concede something nobody claimed and you have built a straw man, which everybody at the table can see. Concede everything and you have simply agreed, and the conversation stops there. What a good speaker gives away is one accurate and limited piece of the other argument, and then qualifies the rest of it.

There is a second half to this, and it is the register. English does the hard part with distance rather than with volume. I suggest that the figure be checked is a more serious challenge than shouting that the figure is wrong, because the construction removes the person from the sentence and leaves only the claim standing there alone. It is essential that this be understood by anybody who wants to argue in English without losing the room. You are not being polite. You are being precise.
reading.source: Article -- The Reader's Column, a weekly newsletter about the press
